findings.problem: Tied wringing to the dry, dusty finish. The World Table Bissap note ties that finish to boiling (seed fragments giving up tannin); its Sorrel note ties pressing to cloud and grit.
findings.change: Dropped “or wrung out”: “Boiled hard, it picks up a dry, dusty finish from the seed fragments.”

findings.problem: The same conflation: wringing said to pull a dusty tannin.
findings.change: Now “which clouds the liquid and leaves grit”.

findings.problem: “Sweeten while warm, then chill hard” read as applying to the hot cup, which goes out with sugar beside it.
No weight or volume, which the style requires of dose.
findings.change: Now “2 to 3 g calyces per cup; sweetener to taste; lime for iced”.

findings.problem: “China, Sudan and Thailand grow most of it” overstates the pack’s Hibiscus component, which calls them the big growers.
Tied wringing to the dull, dusty finish (as in taste).
findings.change: Now: a long rolling boil can add a dry, dusty finish, and wringing adds cloud and grit.

findings.problem: “Careful recipes” called the Library’s full boil and the pack’s agua de Jamaica (calyces boiled eight to ten minutes) careless, taking one side of a disagreement the fragment otherwise gives as a range.
The right option tied wringing to the dusty finish, which the explanation itself contradicts (wringing adds cloud and grit).
findings.change: Now “Boiling adds a dusty finish; wringing adds grit” (47 characters, not the longest).

findings.problem: Checked: the Library card says a full boil, the World Table Bissap and Sorrel steep near 195F (90C) and warn against boiling, and the pack boils agua de Jamaica eight to ten minutes.
findings.change: None. The range 195 to 212F (90 to 100C) and the watch line on the rolling boil reconcile them. Bissap sweetens warm and Sorrel after cooling; the fragment follows Bissap and says to taste again cold, which covers both.
